summary: Grand Bank Wharf light, Burin Peninsula: lit in 1890 from a breakwater beacon, rebuilt in 1922 as the concrete octagonal tower that stands today.

lens.note: Eighth-order dioptric lens at first lighting (LHF). Lantern glass and lens destroyed in part by fire, October 1896; a more powerful lens (sixth order per LHF) placed in April 1897.

structures.note: Original wooden beacon on the breakwater, red and white horizontal bands (LHF). Rebuilt 1920 (LHF).
Present tower on the eastern pier (LHF; Rowlett). Coast Guard list gives 7.1 m.
Grand Bank Sector Light, a separate light on Grand Bank Harbour (Coast Guard list: 9.1 m, fixed red, white and green sectors).

access.note: Coast Guard list and LHF: owned by the Canadian Coast Guard; LHF says grounds open, tower closed. Rowlett says site and tower closed, with good views from the waterfront, and that ownership was being transferred to the town in 2014.

visit.note: Sources conflict on whether the grounds are open (LHF: open; Rowlett: closed).

events.note: Lantern, glass, lens and lamp for a light proposed on the end of the breakwater supplied (Inspector's report for 1881).
Light established 1 May 1890, white light from an eighth-order dioptric lens (LHF). Rowlett: station established 1890.
Fire in the lantern room, October 1896: lantern glass destroyed, lens damaged beyond use (Board of Works report printed 1897).
New, more powerful lens to be placed in position in April 1897 (Board of Works report).
Present concrete octagonal tower erected on the eastern pier (LHF; Rowlett).
Schooner Frank R. Forsey struck the pier and sank; its bowsprit gouged the tower (LHF, citing The Daily News, 12 January 1923).
Converted to battery power in the 1950s (LHF); now solar-powered (LHF).
Ownership being transferred, presumably to the town (Rowlett).

wrecks.outcome: Struck the pier at Grand Bank and sank with a load of salt; refloated when the salt dissolved (LHF, citing The Daily News).

corrections.why: The record's position is the Grand Bank Sector Light (CCG 47 06 04.7 N, 055 45 02.8 W), about 100 m west of the historic Wharf Light tower (CCG 47 06 04.7 N, 055 44 57.8 W, which matches the Wikidata position). The story is about the Wharf Light; a human should decide which position the entry should carry.

corrections.proposed: Split: wooden beacon built 1890 (height not recorded); present concrete octagonal tower built 1922, 7.1 m.
corrections.why: The 1890 structure was wooden (LHF) and was rebuilt in 1920; the 7.0 m height and the 1890 date conflict with the 1922 concrete tower of 7.1 m (CCG list).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Wikidata and Rowlett give 1890 for the first structure and 1922 for the present tower; LHF agrees (1890 wooden beacon, 1920 rebuild, 1922 concrete tower). Consistent once the two structures are separated.
Sources conflict on the grounds (LHF: grounds open, tower closed; Rowlett: site and tower closed). Left unresolved; the record's 'closed' is consistent with Rowlett and the tower.
CCG and LHF say owned by the Coast Guard; Rowlett says ownership was being transferred in 2014, presumably to the town, with the Town of Grand Bank as site manager. Dates of the transfer are unknown.

LHF and the CCG list give a quick-flashing green light (Q G 1s). Rowlett's Grand Bank (East Pier) entry gives a white flash every 4 s, focal plane 8 m. This is a disagreement, and the story states it.

notes_for_editor: Primary checks: the 1881 lantern and lens supplied (JHA 1882), the 1890 'Grand Bank Beacon' spending line (JHA 1891, read by line position: check the page image if the figure matters), the July 1890 inspection visit (JHA 1891), and the October 1896 fire with the 1897 replacement lens (JHA 1897, 'In October last'). The 1889 harbour appropriation is a resolution in the printed journal (PDF p. 224, printed p. 210), not a completed expenditure. Not verified in a primary source: the 1 May 1890 first-light date, the eighth-order lens, the 1891 description, the keeper roster (LHF's list is the only one; no keeper names appear in the Journal reports read here), the 1920 rebuild, the 1922 date, the 1923 schooner incident (LHF citing The Daily News of 12 January 1923: not read; the Daily News was not searched), and the 1950s battery conversion. The record's coordinates belong to the Sector Light (see corrections). Access and ownership conflict between LHF and Rowlett; the story reports both. The Journal's Grand Bank mentions for 1889 to 1912 include many non-lighthouse uses (magistrates, ferries, customs, a 'Grand Banks' fishing ground) and were not used. Wikipedia was read for leads only and is not cited. The Canadian Marine annual reports in the corpus cover Canada before 1924 and do not cover Newfoundland lights, which stayed under the colony until 1949; no Newfoundland primary source was in the corpus. Newspapers were not searched. Fact-check 2026-10-28: the 1889 resolution (JHA PDF p. 224, printed p. 210), the 1891 Board of Works item (PDF p. 495, checked on the page image: Grand Bank Beacon 184 97 in the item column), the 1891 voyage list (PDF p. 631: fourteen stations including Grand Bank) and the 1897 report (PDF p. 325: placed in position early in April) match the story. The 1891 wooden-beacon description is LHF's only; the Journal pages read do not contain it, and LHF cites the Journal for various years without a page. Rowlett places the light at the end of the south breakwater, though its entry is headed East Pier; LHF says eastern pier, and the story gives LHF's position. The 1897 fire wording 'lantern room' is LHF's, not the report's, so the story no longer uses it. The Frank R. Forsey date 12 January 1923 is the date of the Daily News account, not of the sinking, so the wreck date is given as 1923.
